rationale: The original reports mania after celery-root extract in a patient taking venlafaxine and St Johns wort. Later reports do not establish primary hallucination subtype or frequency. Original main body remains inaccessible.
The review describes the same 2016 celery-root case and proposed venlafaxine interaction. It contributes no independent patient or measured visual hallucination outcome.

Original Parkinson drug trial reports aggregate PDQ-39, whose item 33 combines distressing dreams and hallucinations. Individual responses, visual modality and a dried celery-leaf contrast are absent.
Randomized osteoarthritis study of Boswellia plus celery seed extract; pain and general safety, not isolated dried leaf or a measured hallucination frequency.
Review of randomized celery studies on metabolic and blood-pressure outcomes; not an original clinical comparison of leaf and visual hallucinations.

Hypertension crossover evaluates celery seed extract and biochemical safety, not dried leaf; the distinct psychological-outcomes companion is noted separately and does not establish visual hallucination frequency.
Neurological scoping review surveys heterogeneous celery-derived interventions, largely preclinical; it is not an original leaf-versus-control hallucination study.
Same titled hypertensive celery-seed safety trial as rank 3, not an independent cohort; item-level psychiatric safety requires original body.
Same titled hypertensive celery-seed safety trial as rank 3, not an independent cohort; the attempted Research Square body returned 403.

Retracted dyspepsia trial of a multicomponent Persian formula including celery; the abstract does not establish a leaf-only exposure or hallucination outcome. Do not use its results as valid evidence.
Controlled oral celery fruit/seed sexual-function trial, not leaf; no serious adverse events are reported in the abstract, but item-level neuropsychiatric safety requires full original.
Parkinson randomized trial of pharmaceutical dl-3-n-butylphthalide rather than celery leaf; motor outcomes and general adverse events do not provide a measured hallucination-frequency comparison.
